title: An online shop
subtitle: Accept orders during a flash sale without making checkout wait for fulfillment.

nodes.why: The client sends a request ID so retried clicks can be recognized.
Validates the request boundary; authentication still needs an authorizer and application authorization.
Checks stock/business rules and writes a durable order. It returns acceptance, not a claim that shipping is finished.
A transaction stores the order and event record together, avoiding a database write followed by an unreliable separate publish.
A stream consumer publishes outbox changes to EventBridge. Retries mean consumers must handle duplicate business events.
Routes OrderAccepted events to independently managed subscribers. It is not the order database.
The queue absorbs spikes; worker concurrency is limited to downstream capacity. Failed messages go to a dead-letter queue.
Uses the order ID to make side effects idempotent. Payments require their own idempotency and reconciliation.

steps.title: Accept durably
steps.description: Trace one order from the browser to its committed record. A successful HTTP response means the order was accepted.

steps.title: Separate acceptance from work
steps.description: An outbox/stream path moves the event toward fulfillment after the transaction. Design for repeated delivery.

steps.title: Absorb the sale
steps.description: A backlog may grow safely while workers stay within downstream limits. Monitor message age, not only queue size.

pitfalls.title: Bad: synchronous checkout chain
pitfalls.description: Calling inventory, payment, shipping and email serially ties the user request to every dependency and complicates recovery after partial success.

pitfalls.title: Bad: treating delivery as exactly once
pitfalls.description: A retried worker can charge or reserve twice unless the business operation has an idempotency key.

title: A subscription web app
subtitle: Run a conventional application across two availability zones with private data.

nodes.why: TLS protects traffic in transit; user access is checked by the app.
Public subnets in two AZs; health checks choose healthy private task targets. WAF can filter malicious HTTP requests here.
Stateless tasks accept inbound traffic only from the ALB security group.
A second AZ lets the service survive loss of one task location; desired capacity and scaling must be configured.
Private database security group permits only app traffic. Transactions enforce consistency for billing and subscriptions.
This example uses a Multi-AZ DB instance with one standby. That standby does not serve application reads.
Task IAM roles retrieve scoped secrets; rotation needs application connection handling.
NAT enables outbound internet access; endpoints provide private access to supported services. Neither makes the tasks public.

steps.title: Follow a request
steps.description: The internet-facing ALB forwards to private task addresses. The tasks need no public IP for inbound load-balanced traffic.

steps.title: Commit the subscription
steps.description: Both task groups use the database writer. Database failover and application reconnect behavior are separate concerns.

steps.title: Survive an AZ failure
steps.description: Healthy tasks remain in the other AZ. A standby database may be promoted; clients must retry appropriate transient errors.

pitfalls.title: Bad: use the standby for analytics
pitfalls.description: The single standby in this deployment is for failover. A read replica or a different database deployment is needed for read scaling.

pitfalls.title: Bad: put everything in public subnets
pitfalls.description: Public database access unnecessarily broadens exposure. Security groups, private addressing and least-privilege IAM form different boundaries.

title: A video learning platform
subtitle: Upload once, produce streaming renditions, and deliver them near viewers.

nodes.why: An authenticated app grants a short-lived upload URL scoped to an object. Large video bytes go directly to S3.
Private originals remain separate from delivery outputs; lifecycle rules can control retention costs.
An object event starts processing. Record job identity and handle duplicate notifications.
Produces formats and bitrates that suit target players. This is asynchronous work, not a request held open by the web server.
Private origin stores the encoded assets. Access is limited to the intended distribution.
Origin access control protects the S3 origin. Signed viewer URLs/cookies can enforce access to paid lessons.
The player fetches the manifest and suitable segments as network conditions change.

steps.title: Upload without proxying bytes
steps.description: The app authorizes an upload; S3 receives the large file directly.

steps.title: Transform asynchronously
steps.description: An event starts an encoding job. Track failure and completion instead of treating upload success as playback readiness.

steps.title: Deliver to viewers
steps.description: CloudFront caches encoded objects. Viewer authorization and origin protection solve different problems.

pitfalls.title: Bad: public bucket for a paid library
pitfalls.description: A signed CloudFront link does not protect a separately public S3 URL. Lock down the origin too.

pitfalls.title: Bad: one huge original for every device
pitfalls.description: Serving only an original file limits streaming adaptation and can waste bandwidth on constrained connections.

sources.title: Restrict access to an S3 origin with OAC

title: Product analytics without a warehouse
subtitle: Turn raw events into partitioned datasets and answer occasional SQL questions.

nodes.why: Events carry stable IDs, event time and a schema version. Exclude unnecessary sensitive payloads.
Buffers records before object delivery; this is a throughput/cost choice, not instant per-event query visibility.
An immutable source layer enables reprocessing when transformation logic changes.
Transforms data into analytics-friendly files and partitions. Validate schema evolution and late arrivals.
Columnar files and sensible partitioning reduce unnecessary reads. Too many tiny objects can hurt performance.
Describes where datasets live and their schemas; the catalog is not a second copy of the underlying records.
Good for intermittent exploration. Use partition predicates and workgroup controls; results also require governed storage.
Query curated data with scoped access and handle personal-data retention obligations deliberately.

steps.title: Keep an original layer
steps.description: Ingestion creates recoverable source data before business transformations.

steps.title: Make reads efficient
steps.description: A transformation produces compact columnar datasets and useful partitions. Metadata describes the resulting files.

steps.title: Ask focused questions
steps.description: Athena reads matching data from S3. Query cost and latency depend on the files actually scanned.

pitfalls.title: Bad: a crawler is an ETL job
pitfalls.description: Discovering schema does not clean records, rewrite them as Parquet or remove duplicates.

pitfalls.title: Bad: every dashboard scans every raw file
pitfalls.description: Repeated full scans can be inefficient. Curate, partition and evaluate whether sustained analytics merits a warehouse.

sources.title: Athena: partitioning, columnar formats and file size

title: A design studio with on-premises files
subtitle: Keep the existing SMB workflow while storing file objects in S3.

nodes.why: The existing application speaks SMB. It does not need to be rewritten to use an object API immediately.
Maps file operations to S3 objects and metadata. File semantics differ from a general-purpose shared POSIX filesystem.
Writes land locally before asynchronous upload. Monitor capacity and dirty cache during network outages.
Bandwidth governs how fast the backlog drains. A private connection is not automatically encrypted end to end.
Bucket policies and IAM constrain access. Versioning helps recover overwritten objects, subject to retention choices.
Choose transitions based on retrieval needs and gateway support; archived data may need restoration before use.

steps.title: Keep the local interface
steps.description: The application continues to use a share. The gateway translates file activity into object storage operations.

steps.title: Understand the acknowledgement
steps.description: A local write can finish before its upload to S3. Loss of the appliance before upload is a different failure from loss after upload.

steps.title: Match retention to retrieval
steps.description: Versioning and lifecycle have different jobs. Test recovery of old files with the configured storage classes.

pitfalls.title: Bad: call the local cache a backup
pitfalls.description: The cache may contain the only copy of not-yet-uploaded data. It needs monitoring and protection against local failure.

pitfalls.title: Bad: assume unlimited offline writes
pitfalls.description: An outage eventually exhausts local capacity if writes continue faster than uploads. Size the cache for realistic disruption.

title: A booking app surviving a Region outage
subtitle: Explore warm standby, replication lag and the order of recovery operations.

nodes.why: Clients reconnect through the public application endpoint after routing changes and DNS/cache delays.
Health checks can steer traffic, but routing alone does not promote a database or make an application ready.
Compute and dependencies run across AZs. Multi-AZ protects an AZ failure, not every Region-level failure.
Replicate to a compatible cross-Region secondary. The exact replication and failover behavior depends on the database product.
Asynchronous replication can lag. Measure the business impact of losing recent writes during an unplanned promotion.
Warm standby runs an operational reduced-capacity stack. It still needs scaling and dependency readiness before full load.
Fence the old writer where possible, promote the secondary, configure the app, scale and test before routing users.

steps.title: Normal operation
steps.description: The primary serves users while data is copied to a secondary Region. Backups are still necessary for logical corruption.

steps.title: Prepare the secondary
steps.description: Warm standby has working compute at reduced scale. Recovery promotes writable data and increases capacity.

steps.title: Move users after validation
steps.description: Traffic switching is one step in a tested runbook. Measure actual recovery time and lost-data exposure in drills.

pitfalls.title: Bad: DNS failover equals full recovery
pitfalls.description: A healthy HTTP endpoint can still point at a read-only or stale database. Validate a business transaction before declaring recovery.

pitfalls.title: Bad: promise zero data loss from async replication
pitfalls.description: A write acknowledged in the primary may not yet exist in the secondary. RPO is a requirement to engineer and test.
